name: The Āḻvārs (Tamil Vaiṣṇava saint-poets) and their hymn tradition
regions: Vaṭa nāṭu (Tiruvēṅkaṭam and the northern sites sung)

tradition.text: The hagiographies place the first three Āḻvārs at the close of the Dvāpara age and the rest in the first centuries of the Kali age (i.e. several thousand years BCE on the Kali-yuga reckoning from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: c. 6th–9th c. CE (the first Āḻvārs c. 6th–7th c.; Tirumaṅkai c. 8th c. under the Pallava Nandivarman II; Periyāḻvār and Āṇṭāḷ c. 9th c.; Nammāḻvār c. 9th c.)

transmissions_received.what: the Kṛṣṇa and Rāma stories and the Lord's avatāras, sung in Tamil
transmissions_received.evidence: allusions throughout the Prabandham (Kṛṣṇa's childhood, the Bhārata war, Rāma's exile)

transmissions_received.what: Viṣṇu's cosmic deeds and avatāra narratives (Trivikrama, Varāha, Narasiṃha, the churning, the Lord on the serpent in the milk ocean)
transmissions_received.evidence: allusions throughout the Prabandham; the direction relative to the Bhāgavata Purāṇa is disputed (brw:alvar-to-puranic-dravida-devotees)

transmissions_given.what: the four thousand hymns as the Tamil Veda (ubhaya-vedānta); the theology of surrender at the Lord's feet with Śrī as mediator; temple-centred devotion at the divya-deśas; recitation in temple and home
the Prabandham and its Maṇipravāḷa commentaries as primary scripture; Madhurakavi's devotion to the teacher as the model of ācārya-niṣṭhā
the Prabandham as Tamil Veda, read together with the Sanskrit Vedānta (Deśika's Dramiḍopaniṣat-tātparya-ratnāvalī, Munivāhanabhoga)

distinctive_positions: The Lord is Tirumāl/Nārāyaṇa with Śrī (Tiru), supreme beyond all (paratva) and yet easy of access to those who love him (saulabhya: 'eḷiyavaṉ', TVM 1.3.1).
The Lord is fully present in the temple image (arcā) at the sites the Āḻvārs sang (the 108 divya-deśas); devotion is temple-centred and pilgrim.
Knowledge-and-love (matinalam) is itself the Lord's gift, not the soul's achievement ('he graciously gave me knowledge-and-love free of delusion', TVM 1.1.1).
Surrender at the Lord's feet, with Śrī as the one who never leaves his chest, is the refuge of those who have nothing (TVM 6.10.10; Kulaśekhara's Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi 5.1).
The soul's nature is servitude (aṭimai) to the Lord at all times (TVM 3.3.1); the Lord's devotees, of whatever birth, are one's masters (TVM 3.7.9; Tirumālai; Amalaṉātipirāṉ 1).
Love is sung in the voices of Tamil akam poetry: the poet becomes the girl in love (Parāṅkuśa-nāyakī, Parakāla-nāyakī), the mother, the friend; the Lord is sought as lover, child, master and friend.
The divine name, above all 'Nārāyaṇa', is the refuge found after long searching (Tirumaṅkai, Periya Tirumoḻi 1.1).
The Tamil hymns are Veda: Nammāḻvār's four works answer to the four Vedas and Tirumaṅkai's six to the six aṅgas (the tradition's account).

Caste and learning do not measure a devotee: the tradition's twelve include a king, brāhmaṇas, a Vellāḷa (Nammāḻvār), a bard of a community held low (Tiruppāṇ), a Kaḷḷar chieftain (Tirumaṅkai) and a woman (Āṇṭāḷ).
summary: The Āḻvārs — twelve in the tradition's standard list — are the Tamil saint-poets of Viṣṇu whose some four thousand verses, gathered by Nāthamuni as the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham, became the Tamil Veda of the Śrīvaiṣṇavas. Their hymns celebrate Tirumāl with Śrī in his temple images, teach surrender, service and the saving name, and voice love for God through the conventions of Tamil love poetry. Placed here also, as Tamil Vaiṣṇava devotional literature of the same milieu, are the precursor Paripāṭal hymns to Tirumāl and Kampaṉ's Rāmāyaṇa (neither is an Āḻvār work).
notes: Status 'absorbed': the Āḻvārs were not an order; their hymns live on inside Śrīvaiṣṇava temple and home worship (lin:visistadvaita, lin:vadakalai, lin:tenkalai). Some lists count ten Āḻvārs, omitting Āṇṭāḷ (held to be Bhūdevī herself) and Madhurakavi (who sang only of Nammāḻvār).

name: Bhakti-śāstra: the sūtra tradition of devotional theory (Nārada, Śāṇḍilya)
alt_names: Bhakti-mīmāṃsā (name sometimes given to the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra)

tradition.text: Nārada and Śāṇḍilya are ancient sages of the Bhāgavata/Pāñcarātra tradition; the sūtras are attributed to them

scholarly.text: Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtra and Nārada Bhakti Sūtra usually placed c. 10th–13th c. CE or later (both post-date the Bhāgavata Purāṇa on most scholarly views); Vopadeva's Muktāphala 13th c.; Viṣṇupurī's Bhaktiratnāvalī c. 14th–15th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Bhāgavata's teaching of devotion (the gopīs as the model of love; the nine forms; devotion free of the guṇas)
transmissions_received.evidence: NBS 21 names the gopīs of Vraja; NBS 82's eleven attachments overlap the Bhāgavata's forms of devotion

transmissions_received.what: the Gītā's teaching on devotion, cited as scripture
transmissions_received.evidence: the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra argues from the Gītā's words (e.g. that the devotee is 'higher' than ritualist, knower and yogin)

transmissions_received.what: the sūtra form and the opening 'athāto ... jijñāsā'; Bādarāyaṇa cited by name
transmissions_received.evidence: ŚBS 1 imitates Brahma Sūtra 1.1.1; ŚBS names Bādarāyaṇa and Kāśyapa

transmissions_given.what: the definition of bhakti as love and as its own fruit (background to the Gauḍīya prema theory)

distinctive_positions: Bhakti is supreme love (parama-prema) for the Lord, of the nature of nectar/immortality (NBS 2–3); it is supreme attachment (parānurakti) to Īśvara (ŚBS 2).
Bhakti is not a means but the fruit itself (phala-rūpa), higher than action, knowledge and yoga (NBS 25–26, 30).
Bhakti is not knowledge: even one who hates the Lord may know him (ŚBS); knowledge of a king or of food does not please the king or appease hunger (NBS 31–32).
Love must include knowledge of the Lord's greatness (māhātmya-jñāna) and seek his happiness, not one's own — the gopīs' love is the model, the paramour's love is not (NBS 21–24).
Bhakti is attained chiefly by the grace of great souls or by a drop of the Lord's grace; the company of the great is itself won by his grace (NBS 38–40).

Among devotees there is no distinction of caste, learning, beauty, family, wealth or occupation, 'because they are His' (NBS 72–73); the lowest births are eligible (ŚBS, on the tradition of eligibility).
Secondary devotion (gauṇī) is graded by the guṇas or by the motive of the devotee; primary devotion is one, though it appears as eleven attachments (NBS 56, 82).
The devotee should not engage in disputation (NBS 74–75) but reflect on the bhakti-śāstras and keep the virtues (NBS 76–78).
summary: Not an institutional order but the textual tradition of the Bhakti Sūtras: the Nārada Bhakti Sūtra (84 sūtras) and the Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtra (100 sūtras, with Svapneśvara's commentary), which define devotion, rank it above works, knowledge and yoga, name its means and signs, and cite a line of 'bhakti teachers' (bhaktyācāryas: Kumāra, Vyāsa, Śuka, Śāṇḍilya, Garga, Uddhava, Bali, Hanumān, Vibhīṣaṇa and others, NBS 83). Later Sanskrit systematizations of Bhāgavata devotion (Vopadeva's Muktāphala with Hemādri's commentary; Viṣṇupurī's Bhaktiratnāvalī) are grouped here.
notes: Created by U25 as a sub-lineage because the texts themselves name a 'bhakti-śāstra' (NBS 76) and a line of 'bhaktyācāryas' (NBS 83). Parent set to lin:bhagavata-early on the tradition's account (Nārada and Śāṇḍilya as Bhāgavata/Pāñcarātra sages — cf. the Pāñcarātra claim that Śāṇḍilya, not finding the highest good in the four Vedas, received this śāstra, quoted in Śaṅkara's BSBh 2.2.45); this is not a claim of historical continuity. Keeps convergence counts from treating the sūtras as an independent root.
